title: Hot Dog!(s)
summary: Josh and Chuck explore hot dogs: the Hot Dog's consumption habits, what goes into them (trimmings, mechanically separated meat, fillers, sodium and curing agents), how they are manufactured, nitrites and celery powder controversy, organic labeling, history from German Frankfurters and Vienna sausages through Coney Island and Nathan's, the origin of the term "hot dog" at Yale, regional styles like the Chicago dog, Coney dog, and Atlanta-style slaw dog, a University of Michigan study on life lost from hot dogs, and listener mail about the Statue of Liberty crown climb.
topics: origin of the term hot dog

segments.title: Opening banter and hot dog consumption
segments.summary: The hosts introduce the hot dog topic and discuss how they like to cook hot dogs, including grilling versus boiling, beer brats, and how many hot dogs Americans eat per year.

segments.title: What a hot dog is and the USDA definition
segments.summary: Hot dogs are described as a type of sausage, distinguished by finely ground contents and a casing. The hosts read the USDA definition covering cooked or smoked sausage, comminution, and allowed fat, water and non-meat filler limits.

segments.title: Meat content and trimmings
segments.summary: Hot dogs can contain various meats, but the labeling must list byproducts. Beef hot dogs are often made from trimmings, and mechanical separation of poultry and pork is discussed, along with the USDA ban on mechanically separated beef.

segments.title: Sodium, curing agents, and additives
segments.summary: The hosts discuss sodium in hot dogs, curing salts such as sodium diacetate and sodium nitrite, high fructose corn syrup, MSG, liquid smoke, and celery powder used for pink coloring and as a natural nitrite source.

segments.title: Nitrites, celery powder, and organic labeling
segments.summary: Nitrites are linked to cancer risk when cooked at high heat. Celery powder is described as a natural alternative that has the same effect. The National Organic Standards Board voted to keep celery powder on its list of acceptable organic ingredients. Organic and free-range labeling are discussed.

segments.title: How hot dogs are made
segments.summary: The process: grinding meat into a slurry, mixing with spices and ice water in industrial mixers, stuffing into casings, smoking and curing, then peeling casings off and packaging. Regional spice differences are mentioned.

segments.title: History of hot dogs and Coney Island
segments.summary: Frankfurters and Vienna sausages originated in Germany and Austria. German pushcart vendors sold them in New York's Bowery in the 1860s. Charles Feltman started selling in Coney Island and Nathan Handwerker founded Nathan's Famous. Chili dogs and Michigan coney dogs are discussed, plus baseball stadium sales.

segments.title: Origin of the name hot dog
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the name's origin, including a Yale student term from the 1800s and the popular but apocryphal story of cartoonist Tad Dorgan. They also cover xenophobia toward German immigrants and kosher-style marketing.

segments.title: Regional hot dog styles and health
segments.summary: Regional styles are described, including Chicago, Sonoran, and Atlanta-style slaw dogs, and the scrambled dog from Columbus, Georgia. A University of Michigan study estimating that a hot dog shortens life by 36 minutes is discussed.

segments.title: Listener mail on the Statue of Liberty
segments.summary: Listeners Liz McKeller and Jason Marcella describe their experiences climbing the Statue of Liberty crown, calling it unpleasant and crowded. Liz shares tips on photography there.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts thank listeners and give the email address for contact. The show is credited as an iHeartRadio production.
